patch.value: An assignment the scanner cannot read leaves the previous binding standing, so a replaced provenance flag still attests the publish

Measured against a 30-case bypass corpus run through verify() on a throwaway git repository, the canonical auditor admits two unattested publish shapes.

FLAG=--provenance followed by FLAG=$OTHER, then npm publish $FLAG: the shell passes whatever $OTHER holds, but shellScalarsByLine only ever calls scalars.set for an assignment literalScalarAssignments could read. A non-literal right-hand side is not returned at all, and a literal one carrying a shell metacharacter is skipped by the metacharacter guard, so in both cases the loop never touches the map and the earlier --provenance binding survives the line that replaced it. The same holds for FLAG=$(cat file).

The defect is one rule applied in the wrong direction: an assignment the scanner cannot read is treated as binding-unchanged when the shell has made it binding-no-longer-known. Every other unknown in this scanner already fails closed - expandScalars leaves an unknown name in place precisely so that not-understood cannot read as carries-no-flags.

Corpus verdicts, canonical implementation: nonliteral-overwrite=pass (expected fail), nonliteral-overwrite-cmdsub=pass (expected fail); the other 28 cases, including both node-script false-failure controls, are correct.

A non-literal assignment to a name removes that name's binding, so a later expansion of it cannot supply --provenance; A literal assignment whose value carries a shell metacharacter also removes the binding rather than leaving the previous value standing; Reverting the production change makes the new regression tests fail

author: claude

value.author: claude
value.text:
Fixing the reported defect surfaced a third of the same class, unreported until now. FLAG="--provenance;" and FLAG='--provenance;' bind one literal word --provenance; which npm receives as a single unknown argument, so the publish is unattested. The scanner proves attestation by inlining the binding and re-reading the text, and the inlined ; splits the command, leaving a clean npm publish --provenance plus a phantom second command. Confirmed present on origin/main and closed by this change.

The metacharacter rule that would have caught it already existed, but only in shellScalarsByLine. attestation.ts maintains its own scope-aware binding map and never applied it. The rule now lives in one place, readableValue, on the path both consumers read, which is why one change closes both.

A fourth shape was investigated and REJECTED: FLAG=--provenance\; appeared to bypass, but the backslash was consumed by the probe's own JS string literal, so the line under test was the ordinary separator FLAG=--provenance; which correctly binds --provenance. Recorded because the artifact was convincing and would otherwise be rediscovered.

author: claude

value.author: claude
value.text:
CodeRabbit found a fourth fail-open of the same class on review, and verified it against bash rather than asserting it: bash -c 'FLAG=--provenance; NOOP=x FLAG=$(true); printf %s "$FLAG"' prints nothing.

An assignment-only command persists EVERY assignment, so NOOP=x FLAG=$(true) binds both names and leaves FLAG empty. The parser read only the line's first assignment word, so the second was not seen at all and the earlier --provenance binding stood - the same fail-open the fix exists to close, one word further along.

leadingAssignments now walks the whole run of opening assignment words and stops at the first word that is not an assignment, which correctly keeps the environment-prefix case (NOOP=x true) binding nothing. Reverting to reading only the first word fails 2 of the new tests. Corpus grew to 36 cases and reads clean; coverage still 100/100/100/100 across 13 files.

author: claude

value.author: claude
value.text:
Sourcery found a fifth fail-open, this one introduced by the fix itself. The substitution tracker counted parentheses without regard to quote state, so a quoted ) inside $( ) closed the substitution early. The rest of the word then fell outside it, the line read as an environment prefix to a command, and NO assignment was reported at all - so the previous binding stood.

Verified against bash: a script binding FLAG=$(printf ') ' ) leaves FLAG holding the two characters ') ', so a publish expanding it is unattested.

Two changes. Quote state is now tracked inside a substitution, so a parenthesis in quotes is text of the substituted command rather than its delimiter. And an unterminated quote or substitution - where the word's extent is a guess and 'is a command word next' is unanswerable - now reports the assignments as unreadable rather than reporting none, which retires the names instead of leaving a replaced binding standing.

Reverting either fails tests: ignoring quote state inside substitutions fails 1, and returning no assignment for an unterminated word fails 2. Corpus is 38 cases and reads clean; coverage 100/100/100/100 across 13 files.
